Neonates of the freshwater amphipod Gammarus minus emerge from the brood pouch with a body mass of approximately 0.000123 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000123 grams], a value derived from measurements on the congeneric species Gammarus roeselii. This remarkably low mass at birth is characteristic of the genus and reflects the substantial energetic constraints faced by gravid females incubating broods in thermally variable spring habitats. Following release from the marsupium, juveniles pass through a series of successive moults, during which they feed on periphyton and allochthonous leaf litter typical of Appalachian headwater systems. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C], the interval from oviposition to juvenile release is approximately 20 days [ab = approximately 20 days], a developmental period that aligns closely with the incubation durations reported for other spring-dwelling gammarids. By the time of first exogenous feeding, the hatchlings have fully depleted the yolk reserves carried over from the egg, transitioning entirely to particulate organic matter and microbial biofilms.

As growing juveniles progress through the intermolt cycle, they accumulate tissue mass gradually, reaching a sexually immature sub-adult phase before the onset of gonadal activity. The wet weight at puberty, marking the transition to a reproductively viable organism, has been estimated at roughly 0.00182 grams [Wwp = roughly 0.00182 grams] based on scaling relationships established for Gammarus roeselii. This body size at maturation represents a substantial increase from the neonatal mass and highlights the considerable growth investment required to reach reproductive competence. Once an individual attains this critical mass threshold, it begins the process of gametogenesis and, within the same breeding season, may produce its first clutch of fertilized eggs. At a constant temperature of 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C], comparative life-table data from Gammarus roeselii suggest that the maximum daily output of offspring can be approximated from an annual production schedule of roughly 0.247 offspring per day [Ri = roughly 0.247 offspring per day]. This reproductive rate, while modest on a daily basis, accumulates significantly over the course of a year-long breeding period, allowing populations to persist under moderate predation pressure from fish and invertebrate predators.

Adult body size in Gammarus minus exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with males typically attaining a larger ultimate wet weight than their female counterparts. Field-collected male specimens have been recorded with a maximum body mass of 0.0362 grams [Wwi = 0.0362 grams], a value consistent with direct wet weight measurements of large individuals. Females, in contrast, reach a smaller adult mass ceiling of approximately 0.0109 grams [Wwi = approximately 0.0109 grams], which is derived from the relationship between ultimate wet weight and body length assuming a length ratio of 0.67 times the maximum length. This marked difference in asymptotic size between the sexes is a common feature in gammarid amphipods and is thought to reflect the selective pressures operating on male-male competition for access to receptive females. The larger body size of males confers an advantage in precopulatory guarding behavior, during which a male carries a female dorsally for several days prior to her molt and subsequent egg extrusion. The energetic cost of sustaining this guarding posture, combined with the metabolic demands of rapid somatic growth, likely constrains the allocation of resources available for reproductive effort.

The life span of Gammarus minus under natural spring-fed stream conditions has been estimated at approximately 1,095 days [am = approximately 1,095 days] when development proceeds at a water temperature of 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C]. This longevity is comparable to that observed in other cool-water gammarids and is associated with a relatively slow pace of life, including delayed maturation and iteroparous reproduction across multiple breeding seasons. Over the course of this extended adult phase, individuals may produce several broods, with the interval between successive reproductive events being governed largely by the duration of the intermolt period. The maximum recorded reproductive rate, when contextualized as a daily figure, amounts to 0.247 offspring per female per day [Ri = 0.247 offspring per female per day] at this reference temperature, enabling a single female to contribute several dozen offspring to the next generation over her lifetime. However, realized fecundity in the field is frequently lower than this theoretical maximum due to limitations in food availability, competition for high-quality detrital patches, and the risk of injury during agonistic encounters between guarding males.

Populations of Gammarus minus occupying distinct thermal spring systems exhibit subtle variation in life-history traits, although all share the fundamental constraints imposed by a cold-water existence. The age at birth of 20 days [ab = 20 days] and the ultimate wet weight of male individuals reaching 0.0362 grams [Wwi = 0.0362 grams] together define the endpoints of the species' developmental trajectory at the standard temperature of 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C]. Comparative studies with the closely related Gammarus roeselii have shown that the wet weight at puberty, estimated at 0.00182 grams [Wwp = 0.00182 grams], represents a consistent life-history landmark across the genus, suggesting a conserved relationship between maturation size and adult female body mass. The maximum lifespan of approximately three years [am = approximately three years], though relatively short for a macroinvertebrate, is typical for a species inhabiting thermally stable but food-limited spring ecot at a temperature of 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C]opes. Future work examining the interplay between temperature variation and resource quality will be essential for predicting how these shrimp populations may respond to ongoing shifts in groundwater hydrology and riparian canopy cover.
